slides.title: The ladder: which rung is the claim on?
slides.source: Source: Chapter 8, “The ladder of evidence for a shader change”; Chapter 6, mutation run; glossary, Shader verification.
slides.notes: Five rungs from Chapter 8, “The ladder of evidence for a shader change”. The missing-semicolon result is from Chapter 6: 11 checks and 25 of 25 passed while the log said SHADER ERROR.
slides.picture: Five rungs from parse to observation. Only the top rung needs a person with a screen. A broken shader can pass a green suite.

new_texts: Five kinds of proof, each stronger than the last.
0 SHADER ERROR lines in the log
THE LADDER FOR A SHADER CHANGE
Each rung proves something the rung below cannot.
Four rungs run headless. The top one needs a screen and a person.
Five rungs. Each proves something the rung below cannot. Say which rung a claim stands on.

new_texts: What is said works, versus a check that shows it.
Claim: “it compiles”. Evidence: 0 SHADER ERROR lines.
That is rung 1. It says nothing about rungs 2 to 5.
“It compiles” is a claim. Zero SHADER ERROR lines is the evidence, and it proves rung 1 only.

slides.title: Headless shows values, not how it looks
slides.source: Source: Chapter 8, “The ladder of evidence” and “What we did not do”; glossary, Shader verification.
slides.notes: The four renders are a seeded simulation: two software renders match, two GPU renders differ by up to 1 per pixel. Chapter 8 says rung 5, what the GPU drew, needs a person with a display. The 7 bench checks are from the chapter’s run.
slides.picture: Two panels: what a headless run can print, and what only a GPU draws. Then four renders of one image: two on the CPU that match and two on GPUs that differ in the last digit.

new_texts: A run with no window, so no pixels are drawn.
CPU pixels, same on any machine
A dummy renderer draws nothing. The numbers are real;
the picture needs a person at a display.
Headless means no window. It can print values and logic. It cannot judge how the shader looks on a GPU.
all_texts: A run with no window, so no pixels are drawn.
CPU pixels, same on any machine
A dummy renderer draws nothing. The numbers are real;
the picture needs a person at a display.

A software renderer draws on the CPU: identical pixels everywhere.
Two GPUs can differ in the last digit: compare with a tolerance.
A software renderer draws on the CPU, so its output is identical on every machine. GPUs may differ slightly.

slides.source: Source: Chapter 8, “Controlled inputs in a headless Godot run”; Chapter 0, time trap; glossary, Shader verification; glossary, Toolchain.
slides.notes: Free-run frame rates are drawn from a seeded generator between 120 and 170 fps; Chapter 0 measured about 145. 33 frames is the seeded change’s fade length (Chapter 8). Max gaps are computed against the line 1 − t/0.55.

new_texts: A fixed frame rate: every frame the same length.
Free-running: the same 33 frames take a different time each run.
Pinning the clock gives every frame the same length, so the run repeats. Free-running, it does not.

33 frames last 1.10 s at 30 fps, 0.55 s at 60, 0.23 s at 144.

slides.title: Colour or data: the decode changes the number
slides.source: Source: Chapter 8, “Five families”, families 2 and 3; Chapter 7, “Colour versus data”; glossary, Shader verification.
slides.notes: Texel 128 decodes to 0.502 as data and 0.216 as sRGB colour. The flat normal (128,128,255) decoded as sRGB tilts 38.8° and lights at 0.779, matching Chapter 7 and Chapter 8. White at alpha 0.5 over black: 0.5 once, 0.25 twice.
slides.picture: A decode curve with the texel 128 read two ways. Then a flat normal tilting 38.8 degrees when decoded wrongly. Then white at half alpha over black, blended once and twice.

new_texts: A hint: this texture holds colour, so decode it.
keep it as data: a normal map
A colour texture is sRGB-encoded; the renderer must decode it.
Data such as a normal must be read as it is stored.
The source_color hint says a texture holds colour, so Godot decodes it. A normal map must not get it.
all_texts: A hint: this texture holds colour, so decode it.
keep it as data: a normal map
A colour texture is sRGB-encoded; the renderer must decode it.

new_texts: The pixel (128, 128, 255): a surface facing out.
A flat surface should light at 1.000. The wrong decode lights it at 0.779.
Decode the flat normal texel as sRGB and the surface tilts 38.8°, lit at 0.779 instead of 1.0.

slides.title: Golden image, pixel diff and tolerance
slides.source: Source: glossary, Shader verification (golden image, reference image, per-platform reference); Chapter 8, Unity and Unreal comparisons; Unity Graphics Test Framework manual.
slides.notes: Two 16 × 16 images from a seeded generator: noise of up to 2 per pixel plus a 3 × 3 defect of +45. Drag the slider to change the tolerance; counts are computed from the 256 pixels. Pixel diff is not in the chapters; the idea is image comparison against a reference in Chapter 8’s Unity and Unreal sections.
slides.picture: Two 16 by 16 images and their per-pixel difference, with a tolerance slider that changes how many pixels count as different. Then three platforms checked against one reference and against their own.

new_texts: A saved correct picture to compare renders with.
Saved once, after a person checked it. Every later render
is compared with it. A reference image is the same idea.
A golden image is the saved correct output. New renders are compared with it.

slides.title: Loose or tight: false passes and false fails
slides.source: Source: glossary, Shader verification (false positive, false negative); Chapter 8, “Test the spec, not the implementation”.

slides.title: Before you trust a shader change
slides.source: Source: Chapter 8, “What a pass proves” and “What it does not prove”.
slides.picture: A checklist of six items drawn one at a time.

new_texts: Which rung of the ladder is my claim standing on?
Are the inputs fixed: clock, seed and bench?
Does my input separate the right answer from the wrong one?
Does my tolerance catch the bug and still pass good code?
Did I run the test on known-good and known-bad code?
What can a headless run not show, and who looks at the screen?
Then say it exactly: not “check the shader”, but “three pixels within 1 of the model”.
